A call for review process by the City Council requires two council members to initiate an appeal and state a reason for the appeal.
The current process allows a single council member to initiate an appeal without stating a reason, which can lead to unnecessary costs and delays for applicants.

Council Member Ashcroft proposed changing the City Council's call for review process to require two council members instead of one to initiate a call for review and to provide a stated reason for the appeal.
Currently, a single council member can request a call for review of a board or commission decision without needing to provide a reason.
The financial burden of preparing for a call for review falls entirely on the applicant, who must pay a deposit ranging from $750 to $2200, while council members incur no such cost.
In one recent example, a homeowner spent $28,000 preparing for a Planning Board appeal and an additional $4,500 for the City Council appeal, which ultimately upheld the Planning Board’s decision.
Businesses and residents argue that the current system imposes unnecessary delays and costs, deterring investment and development in Alameda.
Supporters of the proposal argue that requiring two council members to initiate a call for review would encourage more thoughtful consideration and reduce frivolous appeals.
Opponents argue that limiting access to the call for review process undermines democratic accountability and transparency, as only elected officials (not appointed boards) are known to the public.
There is concern among some speakers that the current process allows council members to make calls for review without considering the full implications for staff resources or project timelines.
Since 2015, there have been relatively few calls for review compared to the number of decisions made by the Planning Board, with only one call for review in 2017 at the time of the conversation.
If passed, the proposal would necessitate changes to the municipal code, potentially taking 6 to 10 months to implement.
Some council members expressed support for increasing the threshold to three council members initiating a call for review but accepted the proposal for two as a reasonable alternative.
One council member cited past instances where calls for review led to positive outcomes, including modifications to projects or rejection of unsuitable developments.
A motion was made and seconded to revise the process, and it carried with a vote of 3 to 2.

The Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) is seeking approval for a six-year lease with the city of Alameda for a maintenance and operation center on 4.73 acres of undeveloped land and 3.4 acres of submerged lands at West Hornet and Ferry Point streets.

The lease includes a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that establishes a $100,000 holding fund for planning, design, and construction of a new seal haul out, with the city having the right to take over the project if WETA fails to meet deadlines or obtain necessary permits.

The city council requires four votes to approve the lease, while the MOU requires three votes.
The property is zoned for commercial maritime use and is located in an open space district, primarily consisting of tidelands.
The lease agreement does not include provisions for the design of the building, which will be determined through the planning board process and may require three votes for approval.

There are concerns regarding the environmental impact of the project, particularly concerning harbor seals, and the National Marine Fisheries Service is noted as the authoritative body on this matter.
Public input was limited to a November 2010 meeting and subsequent media coverage, with recent speakers expressing dissatisfaction with the lack of community engagement.
The project includes a commitment to mitigate noise pollution by restricting construction and maintenance dredging between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. on weekdays and 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. on Saturdays.

The proposed facility will function as an emergency operations center during regional disasters and support ferry services, including fueling operations using aboveground storage tanks and underground fuel lines.
An oil spill response plan is required for the facility, and WETA has a history of no oil spills in the last 18 years.

The facility will be adjacent to existing ferry operations, including Aida, which previously had an incident involving an oil spill but played a role in protecting the coastline during the ASCO Busan wreck.
The project has been supported by various stakeholders, including the Alameda Chamber of Commerce, the Carpenters Union, and local residents.
